A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Multi-agent Markov Entanglement by the same authors. Their main text, equations, figures, table, and Appendices A–K are readable and support reliable matching, including material reorganized in v3.

before.justification: v1 reports original circulant-RMAB simulations measuring entanglement, local-TD decomposition error, relative error, and convergence with trajectory length in Figures 1–3 and Appendix K.

after.justification: v3 retains the original RMAB simulations and adds original ride-hailing simulation results based on NYC taxi records in Section 7.2.2, Figure 2, and Appendix K.2.

M1.justification: Meta Algorithms 1–2 remain unchanged. New Appendix K.2 introduces application-specific adaptations: pooling homogeneous drivers for entanglement estimation, conditioning optimization on sampled order sets, and learning a shared local state-value function to reconstruct Q-values instead of tabulating the exponentially large state-action-order space.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates only a synthetic four-state circulant RMAB. v3 retains it and adds a ride-hailing simulator calibrated using 810,000 NYC yellow-cab trips from 2024. This introduces spatial dispatching, shared exogenous orders, and driver relocation as actually evaluated conditions; their earlier theoretical discussion was not empirical coverage.

E2.justification: The retained RMAB experiments use the same local-TD results, Monte Carlo reference estimates, and theoretical scaling curves. The ride-hailing experiment introduces no competing decomposition algorithm. Methods cited in the related-work discussion are not newly evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: The added ride-hailing evaluation introduces substantial new settings: aggregation into 15 zones, fleet sizes from 150 to 1,500, 0.1N orders per step, matching that minimizes pickup distance, no travel delays, and idle relocation probability 0.05. Existing RMAB training and testing budgets remain stated as before. Figure 1 also changes the displayed entanglement normalization from N times E1 to E1.

E4.justification: Figure 2 adds a ride-hailing scaling study examining whether entanglement and relative decomposition error decrease with fleet size. The existing 900-agent RMAB analysis of convergence with sample length is retained as the right panel of v3 Figure 3. No new component ablations or distribution-shift tests appear.

E5.justification: v1 Appendix K.2 explicitly states that local-Q training uses 10 independent runs and averages the learned Q-values; v3 removes that statement. The 10 entanglement-estimation runs, 3N Monte Carlo reference runs, and standard-error reporting remain. This establishes a disclosure change, not evidence that the actual repetition count changed.

E6.justification: v3 adds ride-hailing entanglement and relative-error curves, reporting approximately inverse-square-root decay with fleet size and relative decomposition error at or below 3% for large fleets. Existing RMAB curves and trends are retained after accounting for rescaling and relocation. The appendix convergence description changes from within 3N samples to convergence with 5N, although the original convergence plot remains.

T1.justification: The central theorems, assumptions, and appendix proofs remain substantially unchanged; the exogenous-information extension already exists in v1 Appendix J.1. v3 corrects Section 3.3's non-subset statement to strict inclusion and adds ride-hailing estimator derivations and the Q-to-V relation in Appendix K.2. New Equation (20) does not display the discount factor used in the general Bellman equations.

C1.justification: Section 1.1 adds an explicit empirical contribution: demonstrating low entanglement in practical scenarios including ride-hailing. The abstract and conclusion retain the same central claims about exact decomposition, entanglement-based error bounds, index-policy scaling, and efficient estimation.

C2.justification: v3 interprets the ride-hailing decay through conjectured convergence to an asymptotically separable mean-field limit, explicitly leaving rigorous analysis to future work. Appendix K.2 also identifies omitted travel delays as a simulator limitation. These are new explanations and qualifications beyond the retained RMAB interpretation.

D1.justification: v3 adds a simulation-code link and substantial simulator construction information: trip-record period and count, geographic aggregation, order-distribution fitting, toll-based rewards, dispatch rules, and relocation probability. v1 provides no code-access link. Conversely, v3 removes the single-CPU statement, and the new experiment's training budget and uncertainty procedures remain incompletely specified. The linked resources were not accessed.

R1.justification: v3 adds the NYC-TLC data citation and explicitly connects its ride-hailing value-function construction to Online Supply Values in the already-cited Han et al. (2022). The broader positioning against existing value-decomposition and RMAB theory remains unchanged.

P1.justification: v3 makes localized wording and cross-reference corrections, separates Section 7.2 into two named simulation subsections, and reorganizes Appendix K by environment. Most introductory discussion, theoretical exposition, proofs, and the conclusion retain their earlier wording and organization.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands and reorganizes the empirical displays: it adds the two-panel ride-hailing Figure 2 and taxi-zone map in Figure 4, redraws Figure 1's entanglement panel without the factor N, and combines the existing RMAB relative-error and convergence plots into Figure 3. The duplicate absolute-error panel is removed from the appendix but retained in Figure 1.

improvement.justification: The data-informed ride-hailing study provides useful practical evidence beyond v1's synthetic RMAB, while the computational adaptations, code-link disclosure, and corrected Figure 1 presentation improve usability. These gains outweigh the lost RMAB training-run disclosure. However, the simulator omits travel delays, its training and uncertainty procedures are underspecified, and Equation (20) leaves discounting unclear, limiting the strength of the overall improvement.
